+         palette=spectro.colors, colgrid="black", colwave="black", colaxis="black",

+         collab="black", colbg="white",alab = "",flim=c(1,12))

I would appreciate your help

messages.subject: How to create an axis with time units ?
messages.subject_clean: How to create an axis with time units ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
got a question: I would like to display recordings with "real" time units. Let´s say the recording starts at 19:45:00 and ends at 19:46:30 - this should somehow appear as x labels. Any ideas?
Thanks a lot in advance!
Cheers,
Martin
messages.body_snippet:
Dear all,
got a question: I would like to display recordings with "real" time units. Let´s say the recording starts at 19:45:00 and ends at 19:46:30 - this should somehow appear as x labels. Any ideas

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] How to create an axis with time units ?
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] How to create an axis with time units ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

I assume you want to plot a spectrogram. One way of doing so is a bit inelegant but works.

If you're using the regular spectro() function, and assuming 'song' is your wave object:

spectro(song, axisX=F)  ##Don't plot the normal x-axis labels
axis(1, labels = format(seq(as.POSIXct("2013-01-01 19:45:00"), as.POSIXct("2013-01-01 19:46:30"), by = "15 s"), "%H:%M:%S"), at = seq(0,90,by = 15)) ## Add in a new axis on the bottom with labels that correspond to the time you want, and at the places you want them to be.

Here, format() is used to display only certain parts of a time/date object. In our case, only the HH:MM:SS, but you can change that.

If you want to be a bit fancier with the labels, you can specify just the start and the breaks:
start <- as.POSIXct("2013-01-01 19:45:00")
axis(1, labels = format(seq(from = start, to = start + length(temp)/te...@samp.rate, by = "15 s"), "%H:%M:%S"), at = seq(0,length(temp)/te...@samp.rate, by = 15))

length(temp) gives you the no. samples
te...@samp.rate gives you the sample rate
Therefore length(temp)/te...@samp.rate gives you the length of the song in seconds.

This would be slightly different using the ggplot2 spectro function, but I haven't had the chance to explore that one yet (but I'm looking forward to it!).

Steffi

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Very long time of computation with certain files
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Very long time of computation with certain files
messages.body_plain:
HI Daniel,

There are lots of reasons why calculations could take a long time, but one way to speed up the H() or specprop() calculations would be to use a larger spectrogram window length (parameter wl). You would give this parameter directly to the H() function, or use it to create the underlying spec objects which you're passing to specprop().

The default wl is 512. Depending on what you're interested in in these sound files, you might be able to use a significantly larger window. For instance, for certain bird vocalizations without a lot of fast frequency modulation, you could potentially get away with a wl as high as 2048 at your sampling rate of 44 kHz (theoretically cutting computation time by a factor of four). Perhaps a good rule of thumb would be to use a wl that allows you to see details of interest when you display a signal of interest with spectro().

best,
jesse

> objects which you're passing to specprop().
>
> The default wl is 512. Depending on what you're interested in in these
> sound files, you might be able to use a significantly larger window. For
> instance, for certain bird vocalizations without a lot of fast frequency
> modulation, you could potentially get away with a wl as high as 2048 at
> your sampling rate of 44 kHz (theoretically cutting computation time by a
> factor of four). Perhaps a good rule of thumb would be to use a wl that
> allows you to see details of interest when you display a signal of interest
> with spectro().
>
> best,
> jesse

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Relative amplitude not adequate shown
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

I'm not 100% sure what is going on, but I suspect that your file is being normalized before or during the pastew() function. There might be a way to stop that, but I'm not sure exactly how to. Possibly, you might consider looking at the non-normalized amplitude envelope: env(..., norm = F), but that's just a guess.

A work around would be to use the command line program "SoX" to concatenate the files together before comparing them with oscillo() or spectro().  Make sure you have Sox installed (http://sox.sourceforge.net/) and you can call it from R using the sox() function.

To concatenate (or paste together in sequence) your wave files use the following command:

sox("frog1.wav frog2.wav frog3.wav threecalls.wav")  ##this pastes them together into a new wave and saves it to the working directory
calls <- readWave("threecalls.wav")  ##Open the new wave file
oscillo(calls)

Alternatively you could combine them with Audacity, but this could be time consuming if you have a lot to do.

Good luck,

Steffi
